Contributing

Source: .github/CONTRIBUTING.md

Contributions to infernet, whether in the form of issue identification, bug fixes, new code or documentation are encouraged and welcome.

Please note that the infernet project is released with a Contributor Code of Conduct. By contributing to this project, you agree to abide by its terms.

Git

stocnet projects are maintained using the git version control system. A plain-English introduction to git can be found here. I recommend you read this before continuing. A more recent motivation can be found here. It will explain the basics of git version control, committing and repos, pulling and pushing, branching and merging.

Using git from the command line on your lap- or desktop can be intimidating, but I recommend Fork software for Mac and Windows. This allows mostly visual management of commits, diffs, branches, etc. There are various other git software packages available, but this one is fairly fully featured.

The GitHub page allows to access the issues assigned to you and check the commits. You can also access the documents in the repository, although this won’t be necessary after you have cloned it on your computer via Fork.

Identifying issues

Please use the issues tracker on GitHub to identify any function-related issues. You can use these issues to track progress on the issue and to comment or continue a conversation on that issue. The most useful issues are ones that precisely identify an error, or propose a test that should pass but instead fails. Examples for documentation are also most welcome.

Issues that belong to another package in the family should be transferred there rather than fixed here: gh issue transfer <number> stocnet/<package>. See the division of labour below.

Cloning

Once you have downloaded Fork, the first thing you have to do is to clone the remote repository on your computer. Before cloning, you will be able to choose on which branch you want to work: develop or main.

Pull

This command allows you to pull changes from the remote repository to your local repository. Make sure you do that before starting working on your files so you have the newest versions. When pulling, make sure you choose main or develop, depending on the branch you decided to work with. Once you pulled, you have now all the new commits and files and you can start working on your assigned tasks.

Commit and Push

Once you have made modifications on a file and saved them, it will appear in your commit window. Here you can control one last time your file, write the commit message with the issue reference (see below) and commit. Once your commit is ready, you can push them to the origin/main repository. If you are working on a separate branch, it is important to select this branch when pushing to origin/main.

Commits may reference an existing GitHub issue number. Where the issue number is preceded by resolve/resolves/resolved, close/closes/closed, or fix/fixes/fixed (capitalised or not), GitHub updates the status of the issue automatically.

Branching and CI

  • main is the release branch; develop is the working branch (clone/work on develop).
  • PRs into main trigger prchecks.yml: R CMD check (macOS/Windows/Linux), binary build, codecov, lintr, spell check, and PR metadata checks (DESCRIPTION version bump, PR title/description conventions).
  • Merges/pushes to main trigger pushrelease.yml: check, auto-bump version tag, GitHub release with binaries and release notes taken from NEWS.md, then pkgdown site deploy.
  • The PR metadata job requires that each PR into main bumps the Version: field in DESCRIPTION by the appropriate increment, names that new version in the PR title, and itemizes its changes in the PR description under ## subsection titles matching the NEWS.md conventions below.
  • Development dependencies are declared in DESCRIPTION under Config/Needs/build, Config/Needs/check, and Config/Needs/website rather than Suggests — the workflows install them via needs: in setup-r-dependencies.
  • A merge that touches R/model_regression.R or the R/qap_*.R engine files deserves a parse check before it is pushed (Rscript -e 'devtools::load_all()'). The merge that created the current engine silently dropped three function headers and left an orphan function body, so the package did not parse at all.

Design Principles

Project overview

infernet is an R package (part of the stocnet ecosystem) providing the inferential layer for network analysis: conditional uniform graph (CUG) and quadratic assignment procedure (QAP) tests of network statistics, and multiple regression QAP (MRQAP) for network data. Because it builds on manynet, every function accepts matrices, edgelists, igraph, network, tidygraph or stocnet objects, and one-mode or two-mode networks alike.

infernet combines two lines of work:

  • the formula front end, multimodal treatment, and ease of use of migraph’s net_regression(), and
  • the estimator range, missing-data handling, and cognitive social structure (CSS) treatment of Robert Krause’s MrQAP, which is where the R/qap_*.R engine files were ported from.

Division of labour to keep in mind when adding functions:

  • manynet: network classes/coercion (as_*()), making and manipulating networks, and network-level logical tests (e.g. is_directed(), is_twomode()).
  • netrics: everything analytic — marks, measures, memberships, motifs — at the node, tie, and network level.
  • autograph: drawing graphs and plotting analytic, modelling, or diagnostic results, along with deep (often institutional) theming. All plot methods should live there.
  • infernet (this package): testing and modelling, e.g. CUG/QAP/MRQAP.
  • migraph: the software companion to Multimodal Political Networks, holding the mpn_* datasets and the diffusion models. migraph still carries older copies, as net_regression(), and the test_*() family; those are what infernet supersedes, so a fix made there needs porting here, and a fix made here does not need porting back.
  • goldfish: another stocnet package for estimating network event models such as relational event models and dynamic network actor models. Note that these two packages, infernet and goldfish, should reuse similar vocabulary and syntax where possible to improve the “pleasant predictability” of each package.

All stocnet packages aim for the same three things: declarative simplicity, pleasant predictability, and graceful inclusivity. The principles are shared across the packages; the rules and examples below are those of infernet.

Declarative simplicity

Functions should do one clearly named thing with few arguments.

  • Names describe actions, not progenitors. A function is named after what it does, and the authors of a procedure are given in the documentation. A test is named for the null distribution it draws: test_permutation(), test_random(), and test_configuration() rather than names built on QAP or CUG. An estimator is named estimate_<model>(), as across stocnet, so that a user who moves between packages finds the same verb: estimate_mrqap() here, and estimate_dynam() and estimate_rem() in goldfish.
  • Few arguments per function. Every argument is something the user must read about before they can trust the result, so use sensible defaults instead. Example: estimate_mrqap() takes a formula, a network, and times, and everything less common goes through its control list.
  • Features are detected, not declared. A function finds out whether a network is directed or two-mode, and adjusts, so the user does not supply an argument for it. Example: estimate_mrqap() reads directedness from the outcome network with manynet::is_directed(), unless control overrides it.

Pleasant predictability

Users should be able to guess a function’s behaviour from its family.

  • Families share a prefix and their arguments. Example: test_random(), test_configuration(), and test_permutation() all take .data, FUN, and times, in that order.
  • One word means one thing. Function and argument names follow the house rules (see Vocabulary below).
  • A specification can be reused. Models are specified with a formula, so the same specification can be moved between networks and between model types, and its terms (ego(), alter(), same(), sim()) mean the same in each.

Graceful inclusivity

Functions should accept whatever network users bring and return something they can use.

  • Inputs span the common classes. Every function accepts any network that manynet can coerce: matrices, edgelists, and igraph, network, tidygraph, and stocnet objects.
  • Many types of network work. A function should give a considered answer for a signed, a weighted, a directed, a two-mode, a multiplex, a multilevel, and a longitudinal network, and its documentation should say how it treats each type it treats differently (see Input shapes).
  • Missing data stays missing. An unobserved dyad is never read as a zero tie, and a function reports what it dropped rather than quietly shrinking the sample.
  • Only truly unsupported cases fail. Where a function really cannot proceed, the error says why and suggests what would work. Example: dist() on a categorical attribute points users to same().
  • Key steps are reported. Functions say what they did at the verbosity the user has chosen (see Console messaging). Example: estimate_mrqap() reports the family and the directedness it read from the outcome.
  • Results describe themselves. A printed result is short, and carries what the user needs to interpret it. Example: a printed estimate_mrqap() says what was permuted and how many times, how loops were treated, and whether the outcome was read as directed.

Vocabulary

One word means one thing, on both sides of the seam between the formula front end and the engine. The engine was ported from MrQAP and used its own vocabulary; the front end’s words won, since those are the ones users read:

Word Means Not
times how many permutations reps
directed logical, whether i→j differs from j→i mode, "digraph"/"graph"
permute what the null distribution permutes: "predictor" or "outcome" nullhyp, method, "qapspp"/"qapy"
.data the network the user passes in —
matlist the named list of matrices the engine fits data
net one coerced network, inside the formula front end data
reporter the person whose report a CSS slice holds, after manynet’s by column perceiver
bv the reporter index in the dyad-level data, after by pv
testdist a null distribution: the statistics from every permutation or simulation, on a test or a fit dist

mode is reserved for a nodeset, as in one-mode and two-mode, which is what it means everywhere else in the ecosystem. Do not use it for directedness. permute replaced method because “method” says nothing about what differs; "predictor" and "outcome" name the thing that is actually shuffled. data is retired as an identifier: it named the network in one half of R/model_regression.R and the matrix list in the other, one letter away from .data. Reserve data = for the argument a model fitter takes.

When writing documentation or NEWS items, prefer breaking lines at punctuation.

Make it clear when you are referring to functions by adding backticks and parentheses, e.g. a_function(), and arguments by adding an equals sign, e.g. argument=. Argument values or variables can be in double quotation marks, e.g. “value”.

Package architecture

Common commands

This is a standard R package developed with devtools/roxygen2. Run these from an R console with the working directory set to the package root (or via Rscript -e).

  • Load package for interactive development: devtools::load_all()
  • Regenerate docs & NAMESPACE after editing roxygen comments: devtools::document()
  • Run full test suite: devtools::test()
  • Run a single test file: devtools::test(filter = "estimate_mrqap") (matches test-estimate_mrqap.R), or testthat::test_file("tests/testthat/test-estimate_mrqap.R")
  • Full package check (mirrors CI): devtools::check() or rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck()
  • Lint: lintr::lint_package()
  • Spell check: spelling::spell_check_package()
  • Code coverage: covr::package_coverage()
  • Rebuild README.md from README.Rmd: devtools::build_readme()
  • Check every topic is in the pkgdown index: pkgdown::check_pkgdown()
  • Build pkgdown site locally: pkgdown::build_site()

There is no non-R build system — no package.json/Makefile. Roxygen is configured with markdown = TRUE; NAMESPACE and all man/*.Rd files are generated — never hand-edit them. Likewise README.md is generated from README.Rmd — edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

File organization

R/ files are grouped by theme rather than one file per function. The user-facing files are named model_*.R; the internal engine ported from MrQAP is named qap_*.R.

File Contains
model_tests.R the test family: test_random() (CUG), test_configuration(), test_permutation() (QAP), and print.network_test()
model_regression.R estimate_mrqap(), the list path, and the print.* methods for its results, documented on the results page
model_control.R control_mrqap(), which names, defaults, and checks every control of estimate_mrqap(); the old names it converts (.control_renames()) and the options of other models it drops (.control_foreign())
model_results.R the results help page, and tidy() and glance() for netreg and network_test results and for the migraph, ergm, and RSiena results
model_specify.R specify_mrqap(), specify_dynam(), and specify_ergm(): one reader of a formula written for any model, one writer for each model, the record of what each model makes of each term, and tidy() of it
model_formula_ergm.R the to_ergm writer of each term, which specify_ergm() calls
model_formula.R the formula front end: .specify(), .evaluate_spec(), the term registry .formula_terms() and its builders, and specificationAdvice()
qap_engine.R QAPengine() and QAPPermEst() — the one matrix-level engine, for both a dyadic network and a cognitive social structure
qap_shapes.R the four things the two shapes do differently, and nothing else
qap_utils.R formula parsing, input validation, future plumbing, matrix permutation (RMPerm()), the model-fitting dispatcher fit_qap_model(), and the permutation aggregators
qap_css.R what a CSS needs that a dyadic network does not: a vectoriser for a three-dimensional array, and a print method
qap_gmm.R GMM moment conditions and residual functions for the estimator = "gmm" path
qap_gpu.R the optional torch batch OLS path, gpu_batch_ols()
qap_confusion.R probabilistic confusion matrices for binary outcomes
qap_misc.R small combining and reshaping helpers
infernet-package.R package-level doc, global variables, and the shim silencing R CMD check’s unused-import note
zzz.R the attach-time greeting and the cached stocnet version check

Only model_*.R holds exported functions. Everything in qap_*.R is internal, and carries @keywords internal and @noRd. Keep it that way: the engine’s argument names are the MrQAP ones, and exporting them would freeze an interface we still intend to tidy.

Input shapes

Most defects reported against this package are not wrong arithmetic. They are a network shape the function did not expect. Before finishing a function, run it on a signed, a weighted, a directed, a two-mode, a multiplex, a multilevel and a longitudinal network, and decide each case deliberately. Document each decision in the roxygen block with an @section named for the shape, e.g. @section Two-mode networks:.

Missing data deserves particular care here, since handling it well is a reason this package exists. An unobserved dyad is NA, never a zero tie and never a source’s numeric code. make_qap_data() drops NA and diagonal cells before fitting, so a predictor that introduces NA shrinks the sample. QAPengine() counts the unobserved dyads on each variable with .missing_summary() before anything is dropped, reports them, and stores them in fit$missing. The missing control chooses the treatment: "available" (the default) drops them, and "fail" stops on them. Multiple imputation is planned, but it waits for its own design.

Every permutation must use the dyads of the observed model. make_qap_data() recomputes the dyads after each draw, and a free permutation moves the NA cells of the permuted matrix but not those of the others, so the draws used to be fitted on more dyads than the observed model. .missing_blocks() now groups the nodes by which of their lines are wholly unobserved (row, column, and CSS slice), and fixes each node at the end of a scattered missing cell, so that the NA cells map onto themselves. The blocks combine with the user’s groups. QAPPermEst() aborts if a draw uses any other number of dyads, since that is a fault in the engine and not in the data. For permute = "predictor" this needs the residualised predictor to be NA outside the model, and mirrored across the diagonal of an undirected network, which residuals_to_matrix() and residuals_to_array() do.

A tie in manynet’s reserved fixed tie column was set by the design, not chosen, so it is no observation of the process either. It keeps its value, which every predictor built from the network reads. .evaluate_spec() carries it to the engine as the fixed attribute of the outcome’s matrix, from .fixed_ties(), and QAPengine() passes it on as an exclusion mask, exclude, separate from the NA cells: make_qap_data() leaves it out of the outcome’s rows, .missing_blocks() keeps it in place under permutation as it does an NA cell, and .missing_summary() counts it apart, as fit$missing$fixed_ties, so that "fail" does not stop on it. Do not set an excluded cell to NA: that would read a value set by design as an unknown one, which an imputation would then fill.

A structural zero, a cell that cannot hold a tie, is not missing data. manynet does not mark one, so it arrives as an observed zero. The loops that the model leaves out and the upper half of an undirected network are the only cells the engine knows to be structural, and .structural_mask() keeps them out of the counts.

Longitudinal networks

A network that manynet::is_longitudinal() says has more than one wave is a panel, detected rather than declared. .prepare_panel() splits it with manynet::to_waves(), and builds each wave but the first against the wave before it, which .spec_context() holds as ctx$previous. A term whose registry entry has panel = TRUE (inertia, recip, trans) reads that previous wave, and fits without a warning; on a cross-sectional network it keeps its old status. QAPengine(panel = TRUE) draws one order of the nodes for every wave with .permute_panel(), and .panel_blocks() exchanges only nodes whose missing cells match in every wave. A list of networks is never a panel, since nothing says its nodes are the same. Whether a layer term reads the same wave or the previous one is open: see stocnet/infernet#18.

Fixed effects

A bar outside parentheses, y ~ x | sender + receiver, absorbs fixed effects, as in fixest; a bar inside them, (1 | sender), is an lme4 random intercept. .split_fixed() reads the bare bar before stats::terms() sees the formula, so the two never meet. The engine code is in R/qap_fixed.R.

  • A gaussian model is demeaned once. A node permutation maps senders onto senders, and .missing_blocks() keeps the dyads of the observed model in every draw, so a matrix with zero group means keeps them under any draw. By Frisch-Waugh-Lovell, each permutation then fits a plain lm() of the demeaned variables, which is why fixest is only in Suggests. The t-values are rescaled for the absorbed degrees of freedom. A change to the permutations that breaks either property breaks this.
  • Any other family calls fixest in every fit. Logit and Poisson models have no demeaning shortcut. Double semi-partialling still demeans, since it residualises linearly.
  • The intercept is kept as NA. Every result names its first coefficient "(Intercept)", and printing and double semi-partialling rely on that.
  • A group is within its network in a pooled list, nv^sv as fixest writes it, and the same node across the waves of a panel.
  • One word, one meaning. The engine already says fixed for a node that keeps its place and for a tie that the design set, so the argument and the result element are fixed_effects.

Cognitive social structures

A CSS is manynet’s to define, and this package follows it. A network is one where its ties carry a by column naming the reporter, manynet::is_cognitive() says so, and manynet::as_matrix() returns the array the engine fits. Do not build CSS arrays here: df_to_mat() did, and it is gone.

  • Detected, not declared. convertToMatrixList() reads the outcome’s matrix and passes css = TRUE where it has three axes. estimate_mrqap() reports the detection and the number of reporters.
  • Read all three axes. A one-mode CSS from manynet has a slice for every node; a two-mode CSS has rows of one mode, columns of the other, and a slice for every node of both. make_css_data() and .perm_css() read each axis from dim(). The two-mode defect of phase one was a shape read off one axis, and the CSS version of it was the same mistake one axis further in.
  • A reporter is a node. A permutation relabels senders, receivers, and reporters together. For a two-mode CSS the slice order is the row order followed by the column order, offset by the number of rows.
  • Lift predictors to the outcome. A nodal term or a layer that is not a CSS is repeated along the reporter axis by .lift_to_css(). A CSS layer keeps its own reports. tertius() is computed within each report.
  • Missing stays missing. manynet gives a node whose na attribute is TRUE a slice of NA, and those reports are dropped. A slice of zeros that is not so marked could be a report of no ties or a person who was not asked, so .report_css() keeps it and names it in a warning.

Test a CSS change on manynet::ison_hightech, a real CSS whose reports layer is not one, and on the constructed networks in tests/testthat/test-estimate_mrqap_css.R for the shapes and the missing reports it does not have.

Before this merge the two were QAPglm() and QAPcss(), 55% the same code, and every fix had to be made twice. One of them was made in only one place.

Control flows

Bivariate

Test functions consistently:

  1. Compute the observed statistic by applying the user-supplied FUN to .data.
  2. Generate times random, configuration-preserving, or permuted networks via the corresponding manynet generator (generate_random(), generate_configuration(), to_permuted()), rebinding node attributes with manynet::bind_node_attributes() where the statistic needs them.
  3. Recompute FUN over each simulated network.
  4. Return a network_test object recording the test type, observed value, simulated distribution, one- and two-tailed p-values, and the network’s properties (is_directed(), is_complex()).

Multivariate

estimate_mrqap() (R/model_regression.R) is the single regression entry point. Its control flow is:

  1. Read the user’s control through control_mrqap(), so a control that is not named keeps its default, each value is checked, and an old name or another model’s option is converted or dropped before anything is fitted.
  2. Read the formula with specify_mrqap(), which rewrites the terms of other models, drops the terms an MRQAP cannot fit, and names each one.
  3. Dispatch on the input shape. A single network goes to convertToMatrixList(), which parses the formula with .specify() and builds its matrices with .evaluate_spec(); a list of networks goes to .prepare_list_of_graphs(), which converts each network, drops the ones that are missing a predictor with a warning, and pools the rest.
  4. Resolve family = "auto" against the dependent variable (binomial for a 0/1 outcome, gaussian otherwise), and resolve directed and loops from the network with manynet::is_directed() and manynet::is_complex(). Report each resolution with snet_info() so that the user can describe these (default) choices in a paper.
  5. Call QAPengine(), which parses the formula, fits the baseline model once via fit_qap_model(), then runs times permutations and aggregates them.
  6. Attach a probabilistic confusion matrix where the outcome is binary.
  7. Attach the term table, fit$terms, from the parts that .evaluate_spec() records for each column, in the order of the coefficients.

The result is a netreg, with more specific classes in front of it:

Result Class
gaussian c("netreg_lm", "netreg")
any other family c("netreg_glm", "netreg")
a CSS c("netreg_css", <family class>, "netreg")

Write a method at the level where behaviour actually differs, and let S3 fall back for the rest: print() has a method for each of the three specific classes, while autograph needs only plot.netreg() until a CSS wants a plot of its own. The names say what the result is, not the procedure that made it, so they carry no qap, and none repeats a function’s name. A new kind of result gets a new specific class in front of netreg.

Inside QAPengine() the permute control names what the null distribution permutes: "outcome" permutes the dependent matrix only, while "predictor" implements Dekker et al.’s double semi-partialling, running one permutation set per main predictor after residualising it against the others. With one predictor there is nothing to residualise against, so "predictor" falls back to "outcome" and says so. Permuted coefficients and test statistics are then compared against the baseline by compare_perm_to_baseline() and reduced to lower/larger/abs p-value matrices by aggregate_perm_results(), which also keeps the permuted test statistics as testdist. Keep that matrix whenever the summaries change: the summaries are read from it, test-qap_testdist.R checks that they agree, and autograph draws it. The name is the one the test family already uses; sna and migraph call the same thing dist, which autograph’s plot.netlm() reads, but dist() is a formula term here.

One engine, two shapes

QAPengine() fits a dyadic network and a cognitive social structure through the same skeleton. They differ in four places and nowhere else, and those four live in a shape returned by .qap_shape() (R/qap_shapes.R):

Field Dyadic Cognitive
vectorise() make_qap_data(), one row per dyad make_css_data(), one row per dyad per reporter
permute() RMPerm() RMPerm(CSS = TRUE), which calls .perm_css()
unresidualise() residuals_to_matrix() residuals_to_array()
rand_slots sender, receiver, network and reporter

A fifth field, max_trials, says how many permutations to redraw before giving up: one for a dyadic network, since a degenerate draw is simply dropped and counted, and 10,000 for a CSS, whose sparse arrays often permute into an outcome with a single value.

Add a shape rather than a second engine. A random-intercept slot a shape does not list cannot be requested, so a reporter intercept on a dyadic network aborts by name rather than producing a formula that will not parse.

Everything that only one estimator needs is in Suggests: lme4 (random effects), MASS (negative binomial), and pscl (zero-inflated Poisson). The other five are on the branches listed under Parked extensions. A code path that depends on a suggested package must guard with requireNamespace() and abort with an actionable message, and its tests must skip_if_not_installed(). Keeping these optional is deliberate: the common case — a gaussian or binomial MRQAP — must install and run with no compiler and no heavy dependency tree.

Parallelism

Every simulation-heavy function takes times, the number of simulations (default 1000; 1,000–10,000 for publication), and control, which holds the rest. Keep the signature to what the function needs: data, a formula or statistic, times, and control. A user sets the controls once, with control_mrqap(), and gives the same object to every model and test; each function reads the controls it uses and leaves the others alone, without a message. The controls of parallelism are:

  • ncores — a number of cores (default NULL). More than one runs on that many "multisession" workers, and one runs sequentially, whatever strategy says. This is the one to show users first.
  • strategy — a future plan name (default "sequential"; "multisession"/"multicore" for multiple cores), used where ncores is NULL.
  • seed — a number to set the random seed with before the simulations.

Read control with .resolve_control(), so that a list and control_mrqap() are checked the same way. Set the plan with setup_future_plan(strategy, ncores) and restore it via on.exit(). Name an argument that says whether ties from a node to itself count loops, never diag, since diag masks base::diag() in the same functions.

The test_*() family maps simulations with future.apply::future_lapply() and future_vapply(), using future.seed = TRUE for reproducible parallel RNG. The regression engine uses the same setup_future_plan(), and run_permutations() (R/qap_utils.R); use those rather than calling future::plan() from a new engine function.

Progress reporting is not a separate argument. It is read from options(snet_verbosity), so that one option governs how talkative every stocnet package is.

Console messaging

All user-facing messages go through the snet_*() wrappers exported by manynet, rather than base message()/stop()/warning() or cli calls directly:

Wrapper Use for
snet_abort() errors: the function cannot proceed
snet_warn() the function proceeds, but the user should know something
snet_info() notable information about what was done, e.g. a defaulted argument or the method dispatched to
snet_minor_info() incidental detail
snet_success() confirmation that a requested operation completed
snet_unavailable() not-yet-implemented features

Every wrapper except snet_abort() is silenced by options(snet_verbosity = "quiet"), which is the default — so informational output must never be load-bearing, and errors must carry everything the user needs to act. Users opt in with e.g. options(snet_verbosity = "verbose").

These wrappers pass their input to cli, so:

  • Braces interpolate, replacing paste(): snet_abort("{.val {dep}} is not in the data.").
  • A brace expression beginning with a dot is read as a style, not as code, so {.val {.directed_label(x)}} aborts with “Invalid cli literal”. Resolve a call to a dot-prefixed function into a local variable first.
  • snet_info() pastes its arguments, so pass separate strings for a longer message rather than a named c() vector: the names are dropped and the strings run together without a space.
  • Use cli inline classes to mark up what you refer to — {.fn} for functions, {.arg}/{.var} for arguments and variables, {.val} for values, {.pkg} for packages, {.url} for links.
  • Use cli’s pluralisation rather than hand-written branches: snet_warn("Dropped {length(dropped)} network{?s}.").

Prefer “{.arg times} must be a positive whole number” over “invalid input”.

Report every default the model resolves for itself, with snet_info(): the family read from the outcome’s values, the directedness read from the network, and any fallback such as permute = "predictor" reducing to "outcome". A model the user did not state is one they cannot describe in a paper. Because this output is silent by default, a broken message is invisible in every other test, so cover it in tests/testthat/test-qap_reporting.R, which runs with snet_verbosity = "verbose". Check a message there with expect_any_message() from helper-infernet.R rather than expect_message(), which lets every other message of the call through to the console. Where a function needs a package from Suggests, name it and say how to get it: snet_abort(c("The {.pkg lme4} package is required for random effects.", i = "Install it with {.run install.packages(\"lme4\")}.")).

The model specification advice printed by specificationAdvice() is informational, not load-bearing, so it belongs at snet_info().

Formula conventions

A formula is meant to be reusable across models and across stocnet packages, even if the calculation or interpretation may differ across models. Currently only infernet, goldfish, and ergm use a formula. This section records the rules infernet follows and how terms might correspond to those in other packages.

infernet goldfish ergm RSiena MoNAn

Rules

  1. A term is a function named for the matrix or statistics it builds. Its first argument is a bare name, and options are named arguments that can also be given by position.
  2. The left-hand side names the outcome layer. . means the layer the network declares as info$focal (in stocnet objects), or the whole network where it declares none. A named left-hand side takes priority over info$focal.
  3. A bare name is a layer, tie attribute, or dyadic covariate. Both layer and tie(layer) work, and tie() gives 0/1 unless weighted = TRUE. Where no layer or tie attribute has the name, a term that can stand alone is that term with its defaults, so ~ recip reads the outcome’s reverse tie, as goldfish’s endogenous recip does. A name that is both a layer and such a term aborts. The argument of a term is read by the term’s kind: a node attribute for ego(), a layer for indeg().
  4. : and * make interactions of any order. These are the product of the operands. An operand with several columns, e.g. same(x, diff = TRUE), gives one product for each.
  5. A two-mode attribute is read on the mode of each side.
  6. A term a model cannot fit is dropped, and the model says why. A formula written for another model should still run here, without the terms this model cannot fit, so that it does not stop the investigation. specify_mrqap(), which estimate_mrqap() calls on every formula, drops them with one warning that names each term and the reason, and the rest is fitted. It rewrites a term that has an MRQAP equivalent, such as ergm’s nodematch("dept") as same(dept), and names a term that means something different here, such as goldfish’s sim(), with snet_info(). An interaction with such a term is dropped whole. specify_dynam() and specify_ergm() do the same for goldfish and ergm. Each reads the formula into infernet’s terms, and then writes them for its model, so a new model needs one reader and one writer, not a translation from each of the others. For example, since MRQAPs rely on permutation, goldfish’s inertia or trans, which read the outcome’s own ties, are dropped. A formula aborts only where a name is known to no model, which is probably a typing error and gets the nearest name as a suggestion, where no term is left, or where a term is refused: tie() and indeg() of the outcome layer would predict the outcome from itself, and same() twice on one attribute, since the columns of same(x, diff = TRUE) add up to same(x).
  7. A column name joins its parts with underscores. The term comes first, then its layer, attribute, and category: ego_age, indeg_friends, tertius_friends_age, same_dept_sales, and mix_dept_sales_hr (the sender’s category, then the receiver’s). indeg(friends, type = "ego") gives ego_indeg_friends. A character that a name cannot hold, such as a space in a category, becomes one underscore, and an interaction joins its columns with :. The name is a label: since attributes and categories can hold underscores, do not parse it back into its parts. The parts are kept instead in the fit’s term table, fit$terms, one row for each coefficient, and tidy() adds them to the estimates: effect (the term, such as "same", or "intercept" or "interaction"), layer, attribute, category as the data hold it, reference, and, for an interaction, operands, the columns it multiplies. A mix() pair is written as a tie is in DOT, "sales -> hr", or "sales -- hr" where the pair is unordered. A categorical ego(), alter(), or mix() names its reference category in a message and in the term table, not in each column. term is the column’s name, as in broom; goldfish’s coef_layout() calls the same field name.
  8. A categorical term leaves out a reference only where its columns cover every dyad. Columns that cover every dyad add up to the intercept, so one of them must be left out. ego(), alter(), and mix() cover every dyad, and leave out their first category or pair. same(x, diff = TRUE) does not: a dyad of two different categories is in none of its columns, and is the reference, so it keeps a column for every category. An option of an existing term is preferred to a new term where the columns mean the same thing, as ergm’s nodematch(diff = TRUE) is; mix() stays its own term, since most of its pairs are not the same.
  9. levels = chooses the categories that get a column, as in ergm. ego(), alter(), same(), and mix() take it. Its values are names, or positions in the order of the columns, where negative positions leave those out, as ergm’s levels = -1. A name is a category as the data hold it, or for mix(), a pair as the term table writes it, "sales -> hr"; mix() reads pairs with levels =, where ergm uses levels2 =, and orders them as ergm does, the sender’s category changing fastest, so that the positions agree. The categories left out are the reference together, by rule 8; where every one is chosen, the first chosen is. An unknown name aborts and lists the categories. A term with more than ten categories and no levels = warns, as goldfish plans to (stocnet/goldfish#122).

The dictionary

The MRQAP column is what estimate_mrqap() does with the term: it fits it, it fits it and warns, it drops it and fits the rest, or it refuses the formula. The registry .formula_terms() holds the same for each term (mrqap), with the term’s name in the other models, and a test checks that every registered term has a row here. The registry names each model, not its package: dynam for a DyNAM or REM in goldfish, saom for RSiena, and ergm.

Each specify_*() function records what its model makes of each term of a formula, and tidy() returns that record. The statuses are one vocabulary, .statuses(), for every model: fits, adapted (rewritten as the model’s equivalent), interpreted (kept, but the model defines it differently), warns, drops, and refuses. test-model_specify_record.R holds the expected status of every registered term in every model.

The ergm column is also what specify_ergm() writes each term as, through the term’s to_ergm function in the registry: the first ergm term named, or else edgecov of the matrix that infernet builds. An undirected network reads ego() and alter() as nodecov or nodefactor. A term with no ergm name, or with an ergm name but no to_ergm, such as common_sender, is dropped. A cognitive social structure and a list of networks abort.

infernet / goldfish MRQAP Meaning ERGM (ergm) SAOM (RSiena) MoNAn

goldfish’s endogenous effects read the dependent events where no network is named. In an MRQAP, such a term reads the outcome’s own ties, which permuting the outcome does not permute with it, so it is dropped. trans(friends) names another layer, and goldfish would read that layer instead. It is also dropped for now, since its matrix is not yet built here, and the warning says so.

Two terms still differ from goldfish:

  • goldfish defines sim(x) as -transformer_fn(x_i - x_j), with abs by default, where infernet uses 1 − |d| / range.
  • goldfish includes ego in tertius() and tertius_diff(), where infernet reads only j’s other in-neighbours.

Adding a term

  1. Add an entry to .formula_terms() in R/model_formula.R: its formals, its kind, its builder, whether it accepts a two-mode network, what it does with the outcome layer, its MRQAP status (mrqap, with a reason where it warns or drops), its nearest DyNAM, SAOM, and ERGM terms (dynam, saom, ergm), and its writer for ergm (to_ergm, in R/model_formula_ergm.R). A term whose meaning or name differs in goldfish also needs a line in .dynam_operand() or .interpreted_dynam() in R/model_specify.R. A term of another model that MRQAP cannot fit goes in .dynam_terms() with mrqap = "drops" and a reason, and needs no builder.
  2. Write the builder. It takes the parsed operand and the context, and returns a named list of matrices: one for most terms, several for a term like match(). .evaluate_spec() lifts each to a CSS array where needed. .build_operand() records each column’s term, layer, and attribute from the term’s kind. A builder that knows more, such as each column’s category, gives it in a parts attribute of the list it returns.
  3. Add a row to the dictionary above, with its MRQAP status, a row to expected_status in test-model_specify_record.R, with its status in each model, and a test to test-formula_terms.R that checks the matrix against a value computed by hand or by a loop.
  4. Add the term to the formula parameter of estimate_mrqap().

Preparing Contributions

Tests

This package uses the testthat package for testing functions. Please see the testthat website for more details. testthat edition 3 with parallel execution is configured in DESCRIPTION (Config/testthat/parallel: true). Config/testthat/start-first should prioritise the test files that take longest to run.

Tests in tests/testthat/ mirror the R/ files for the exported functions (test-estimate_mrqap.R, test-model_tests.R), and are grouped by contract for the engine:

File Asserts
test-qap_estimators.R each family and random-effect combination, against the equivalent standard fit
test-qap_shapes.R the dyads that reach the model, for each shape of network
test-qap_reproducibility.R that a seed reproduces a run, sequentially and in parallel
test-qap_control.R the control list and the choice of null hypothesis
test-qap_reporting.R the messages that report what the model resolved, with verbosity on
test-qap_shape_css.R the CSS shape of the engine, on hand-built arrays
test-qap_panel.R a longitudinal network as a panel: the waves, the lagged terms, one permutation for every wave, and its missing cells
test-qap_missing.R that every permutation keeps the missing cells, and so the dyads, of the observed model, for each shape, and the missing control
test-estimate_mrqap_css.R CSS models through estimate_mrqap(), from manynet networks
test-qap_testdist.R that the p-values can be read back from the stored null distribution
test-formula_spec.R the grammar: named arguments, interactions of any order, the outcome, and refused formulas
test-model_specify.R what the terms of each model become in each specify_*() function, which are dropped, and how the model a formula was written for is read
test-model_specify_record.R the status each model gives each registered term, the record of each term, tidy() and the columns it names, and formulas from goldfish’s documentation
test-model_specify_ergm.R specify_ergm() with a network: each term’s ergm term or edgecov() matrix, two-mode and undirected networks, and an ergm fit of the result
test-formula_terms.R each term’s matrix against a value computed by hand, and the dictionary
test-model_results.R tidy() and glance(), on hand-built results and on fits
test-tutorials.R that the code of each tutorial in inst/tutorials/ runs without error

tests/testthat/helper-infernet.R holds the shared fixtures and expectations:

  • qap_net_gaussian(), qap_net_binary(), qap_net_count(), qap_net_zip(), qap_net_undirected(), qap_net_twomode() — each seeded, and each carrying real signal, so that every family converges and the comparison is not testing noise against noise.
  • formula_net() — a six-node multiplex network with two layers, small enough that a term’s matrix can be checked by hand.
  • qap_reference_data() — rebuilds the dyad-level data frame the engine fits, so a baseline coefficient can be compared against lm(), glm(), MASS::glm.nb(), pscl::zeroinfl(), lme4::lmer() or fixest::feglm() on identical data.
  • expect_qap_shape() — the shape contract every estimator meets, whatever it fits underneath: named coefficients, and lower/larger/abs as two-row matrices of proportions with matching dimnames.

Four things are worth asserting for every estimator that is added:

  1. That the baseline coefficients match those of the equivalent standard fit on the same dyad-level data, using qap_reference_data(). The permutation inference is what is novel; the point estimates are not, and they should agree.
  2. That the result meets expect_qap_shape(). Most engine defects found so far surfaced as a name or a dimension, not as a wrong number: a backticked coefficient name broke double semi-partialling, and a stray placeholder intercept broke the fixest path.
  3. That a given seed reproduces the same p-values. Permutation results are only comparable across runs if the RNG is, and future.seed = TRUE is what makes that true in parallel.
  4. That the estimator is reached at all. Several paths in fit_qap_model() are selected by a combination of family, estimator and the random/fixed effects flags, so a test that does not name that combination does not cover it.

An estimator that needs a package from Suggests takes skip_if_not_installed(), so the suite still passes where that package is absent. Do not let a path go untested because the package is missing locally: install it, and check that the test runs before you rely on the skip.

Note that skip_if_not_installed() is weaker than it looks. CI installs every Suggests, so the skip does not fire there, and an installed package is not always a working one: torch installs as an R package before its Lantern backend is downloaded, and torch::cuda_is_available() then throws rather than returning FALSE. Guard on the capability, not on the package.

A test must not depend on a manynet feature newer than the CRAN version, or it passes here and fails on CI.

Note that options(snet_verbosity) is unset under R CMD check, because manynet’s .onAttach only sets it in an interactive session. Never write a test that depends on snet_info() output.

Count the dyads rather than checking that a call returns. A directed network of n nodes contributes n(n-1) dyads, an undirected one n(n-1)/2, and a two-mode one every cell of its incidence matrix. Each of those was wrong at some point, and each looked like a working model.

A fitter’s warning raised inside the permutation loop is held back, since it would print once per draw; aggregate_perm_results() reports the number of draws that failed outright. A test therefore should not expect a convergence warning from a permutation, only from the baseline.

The aim is to work towards comprehensive coverage, so each change should be fully covered by tests. However, we also need to keep an eye on the clock: CRAN complains if tests take too long, so use small fixtures, low times, and skip_on_cran() for taxing tests. # nocov start and # nocov end can be used to exclude lines or functions that are too difficult to cover.

Documentation

Roxygen is configured with markdown = TRUE; NAMESPACE and all man/*.Rd files are generated — never hand-edit them. Run devtools::document() after changing any roxygen comment.

  • Related functions share one roxygen block via @name/@rdname, matching the file organisation above.
  • Document each argument once. estimate_mrqap() takes its options through a control list, and each control is a formal argument of control_mrqap(), documented there with its own @param. To rename a control, rename the argument and add the old name to .control_renames(), so that a script with the old name still runs and is warned. A stray @param for something that is no longer a formal argument is an R CMD check warning, and the duplicated blocks that the engine merge introduced were exactly that.
  • Every exported function needs a runnable @examples block: examples are run by R CMD check, and they are also the fastest documentation for users. Prefer the bundled ison_*/fict_* networks from manynet over ad hoc constructions, and keep times small so the example is fast.
  • Use the native pipe |> in examples, never %>%. migraph shipped examples that called %>% after the re-export was removed, and every one of them failed R CMD check.
  • Cite the source of a method with @references in the ecosystem’s format (authors, year, title, journal, and \doi{} where available), so that users can trace an implementation back to its definition.
  • Documented behaviour and implemented behaviour must agree. When you change a default, search the roxygen for it too.

README and website

The README offers a landing page for new users, both on the GitHub repository as well as on the website. As such, it should make a compelling case for the value added of the package, and not drift out of date. Note that README.md is generated from README.Rmd — edit README.Rmd and re-knit (devtools::build_readme()), never edit README.md directly.

The website is created by pkgdown from pkgdown/_pkgdown.yml, and is deployed automatically when changes reach main. Please make sure that the pkgdown website will build correctly before opening a PR:

pkgdown::check_pkgdown()              # every topic is in the index
pkgdown::build_site(preview = FALSE)  # everything else

The most common failure is a new exported function that is not picked up under the function overview (the reference: section of _pkgdown.yml) — pkgdown requires every exported topic to appear there exactly once, or it will not build. A helper that users are not meant to call takes @keywords internal instead. These reference: titles are also the headings used in NEWS.md (see below), so keep the two in step.

NEWS.md conventions

NEWS.md groups each version’s changes under ## headings that mirror the website function overview (pkgdown/_pkgdown.yml reference: titles). Lead with ## Package (package-wide/website/infrastructure changes), then ## Tests (the test_*() family) and ## Regression (estimate_mrqap() and the engine behind it). Each heading appears at most once per version.

Start each bullet with a verb matching the change type:

  • Added ... — new functionality
  • Fixed ... — bug fixes; if it relates to a GitHub issue, suffix with (closing #123)
  • Renamed ... to ... — function or data name migrations
  • Improved ... — functional updates to existing behaviour
  • Updated ... — documentation changes

If a cited GitHub issue was not authored by @jhollway, thank the author with an @-tag in the bullet.

Grouping

Group first, and only then write the bullets. The more entries a version holds, the more this matters.

  • Cluster related changes as indented sub-bullets under a lead bullet.
  • Where several changes concern one function, lead with an Improved ... bullet naming the function, and put the individual Fixed .../Added ... points beneath it, so the cluster groups by function rather than by change type.
  • Under such a lead bullet, do not name the function again in the sub-bullets, since the lead bullet already carries it.
  • Where one decision runs across many functions, lead with the decision rather than with each function.
  • Sub-bullets indent by two spaces, and nest at most one level further (four spaces).

Writing the bullets

NEWS.md is read by users scanning for what changed, not by reviewers reading prose, so each bullet is a headline rather than a sentence, so avoid over-punctuation or over-explanation. Details can be added to the function documentation, if necessary.

  • No full stop at the end of a bullet
  • Keep every bullet to one line of fewer than 81 characters ideally (a few more or less is fine)
    • If a bullet wraps, it holds too much: shorten it, or split it into a lead bullet and sub-bullets
  • One clause where possible, and at most one comma
    • Use a semicolon for a short second clause, e.g. “old spelling still works but warns”
    • Use a sub-bullet where the second clause needs more room than that
  • Name the function or object in backticks and say what changed to it, dropping scaffolding like “This change …”, “In order to …”, or “as part of an effort to”
  • Keep the what, and add the why only where the behaviour would otherwise look arbitrary
  • No trailing rationale, no restating the same change twice in different words, and no marketing adjectives such as “comprehensive” or “robust”
  • A sub-bullet does not need a verb: it can state the consequence, the previous behaviour, or an example call
  • Cut a sub-bullet that only restates what the lead bullet already implies
  • Where several bullets describe parallel changes, reuse the sentence structure, so that a reader sees the parallelism at a glance
  • Use one word for one thing throughout a version’s entries, rather than varying the wording for effect

For example, instead of:

Fixed a bug where, in some cases, print.network_test() was not returning its input invisibly, which meant that x <- print(test) assigned NULL.

write:

Fixed print.network_test() to return its input invisibly

and instead of:

Added a new control option, use_gpu, which is a useful option that allows the permutations to be run in batch on the GPU using torch.

write:

Added use_gpu control for batch OLS permutations on the GPU
